notes.headline: Petrobras: record output of 3.51 million barrels a day lifts profit 22%, but earnings miss forecasts and spending rises sharply
notes.takeaway: Net income rose 21.5% to R$39.8 billion ($7.7 billion) on record production, a 99% refinery utilisation rate and higher oil prices, but missed the R$46.6 billion consensus. Petrobras raised its 2026 production forecast to 3.3–3.4 million barrels a day and its capital spending forecast to $24–25.5 billion, and the ADRs fell 2.9%.
results: Petrobras reported net income of R$39.8 billion (US$7.7 billion) for the third quarter, up 21.5% from a year earlier, according to its results and press reports. Excluding one-off items, net income was R$47.9 billion, up 68%. Revenue in dollar terms rose about 40%.

Oil and gas production averaged a record 3.51 million barrels of oil equivalent a day, about 2.96 million of it from the pre-salt fields, the third quarterly record in a row this year. The company brought new floating production vessels on line ahead of schedule and received authorisation to run 11 platforms above their original capacity. Refineries ran at 99% utilisation and diesel output hit a record.

For the first nine months net income rose about 46% in dollar terms to roughly $24.4 billion. The company also announced the purchase of the remaining 70% of Logum, an ethanol pipeline company, for R$620 million.
mgmt: Chief executive Magda Chambriard said the company again achieved record oil and gas production and record diesel output with refinery utilisation of 99%, which she said was essential to Brazil’s energy security during the geopolitical crisis, and that strong cash generation is funding faster execution of investments.

Petrobras raised its 2026 production forecast to 3.3–3.4 million barrels of oil equivalent a day from about 3.1 million, lifted its expected operating cash generation for the year to $45–50 billion from about $35 billion, and raised its capital spending target for projects under implementation to $24–25.5 billion from about $19.4 billion.
view: Operationally, this was one of the best quarters in Petrobras’ history. Producing 3.5 million barrels a day — up more than 10% in a year — while running refineries flat out shows a company executing its offshore development plan faster than promised, helped by the Búzios field and new platforms. The ability to push existing platforms above nameplate capacity is particularly valuable because it adds barrels without new investment.

The disappointment is in the conversion of that production into earnings and in how the cash will be used. Profit fell short of forecasts despite high oil prices, and Petrobras’ domestic fuel pricing — where the government-controlled company has historically been slow to pass international prices through to Brazilian consumers — remains a structural limit on how much of a price spike reaches the bottom line. More importantly, the 30% increase in the spending target signals that the cash windfall is going into new projects rather than to shareholders. Under President Lula’s government, Petrobras has expanded into refining, fertilisers and renewables, which the market views as lower-return uses of capital.

That is the permanent tension in Petrobras: a world-class, low-cost producer of deep-water oil that is also an instrument of national policy. The shares trade at a low multiple of earnings with a high dividend yield, reflecting that tension rather than the quality of the assets. Investors get exceptional production growth and large dividends while oil prices stay high; the risk is that a fall in crude prices meets a higher spending commitment, squeezing the payouts that justify owning the shares.
notes.watch: Watch the fourth-quarter dividend declaration, the next five-year business plan, domestic fuel-pricing decisions, and production from the new platforms.
